Training can become unstable when updates are too large
relative to sharp directions of the loss landscape, so that they
overshoot rather than converge toward a minimum [10], [11].
Stochastic extensions, such as the break-even point framework,
relate instability to both sharpness and curvature variability,
particularly during an early phase in which learning rate and
batch size shape the subsequent trajectory [12]. The Edge-
of-Stability literature, however, shows that deep networks
often continue to make progress near, or even beyond, the
nominal sharpness threshold [13]–[15]. These works provide an
important geometric interpretation of training dynamics. They
also motivate a complementary question: how does one update
interact with the next, and how do their repeated interactions
affect learning? A trajectory can repeatedly reverse in some
directions while continuing to descend in others. Explaining this
behavior requires following both the magnitude and direction
of the steps actually taken, rather than treating every oscillation
as failed progress.

D. Checking the Curvature Estimate
The smooth tanh MLP allows a direct check of the estimated
curvature. We independently compute Hessian–vector products
along the same sampled gradient direction and compare them
with Eq. (15). The comparison shows why the sampling term
matters: correcting for the measured noise brings the two-
gradient estimate much closer to the independent curvature
calculation across all stochastic batch sizes. Supplementary
Table S2 and Figs. S1–S2 give the paired errors and the separate
frozen-parameter sampling check.
Curvature agreement and accurate loss prediction are differ-
ent questions. On a nonlinear objective, curvature can change
during a large step, and the local quadratic loss relation can then
give the wrong sign. We retain the complete sign comparison
in Supplementary Table S1. Accordingly, the figures are
interpreted through direction, magnitude, and observed loss
together; the reference value two is not used as an unconditional
prediction of the next loss increase.

accompanied by a growing gradient has a larger opposing
component, which appears as a larger Qt. In ResNet and the
Transformer, pronounced excursions are followed by intervals

The same consecutive-gradient argument helps interpret these
Adam trajectories. They do not transfer the SGD quadratic
threshold into an Adam stability guarantee: Adam changes the
magnitude and direction of the parameter increment through
its moments. The question is empirical—how often do the
gradient conditions precede an observed loss increase, and
does the association become clearer for larger increases?
To answer it, write Lt = L(θt) and evaluate each condition
at θt, after computing gt but before applying the next update.
The next-step outcome is Lt+1−Lt. Table II compares negative
cosine, norm growth, their conjunction, and Qt ≥2 for
individual loss increases of at least 10%. Coverage counts how
many such increases satisfy the condition beforehand. Precision
asks the reverse question: among all times the condition holds,
how often does such an increase follow? Both are needed
because a condition can cover many increases simply by
remaining active for much of training.
Reversal covers most or all of these increases, while requiring
growth makes the condition more selective. The stronger Qt
condition trades coverage for precision; it is a combination of
the same two gradient measurements, not a separate source
of evidence. Neither condition is universal: the complete
audit retains missed increases and occurrences followed by
decreasing loss.

B. Tracing Oscillations through the Learned Function
A parameter update changes the representations computed
at successive layers and, eventually, the network output.
If gradients repeatedly reverse, we can ask whether these
functional changes also move back and forth, whether their
magnitude grows during a loss excursion, and how widely
the behavior is shared across the network. Answering these
questions requires comparing the network on the same inputs.
Otherwise, a representation difference could arise simply
because the examples changed.

1) Where the oscillation appears: Figure 6 aligns loss,
change direction, and movement size on the same training-
step axis. Reading downward connects a visible loss excursion
to what happens inside the network. Reading upward from
the output asks how far back the same behavior is already
present. The displayed endpoints summarize the architecture
without averaging away the changes within each measured
representation.
In the MLP, the middle heatmap is negative throughout
the selected window, beginning at the first affine layer. Its
representations keep reversing while the loss both rises and
falls. The lower heatmap shows that the size of these reversals
varies considerably; the tanh layers attenuate the movement
transmitted by the preceding affine layers. The separate stage
normalizations show when each representation moves most,
not its absolute size relative to another stage. Thus the loss
excursion occurs within an already oscillating network, rather
than requiring a newly appearing reversal at its peak.
The larger ResNet excursion is accompanied by a coordinated
increase in representation displacement across the measured
stages. The first convolution reaches its largest change near the
loss peak, followed by the later stages. Their change directions
become increasingly similar to the output’s behavior toward
the end of the network. In the Transformer, by contrast, later
representations can reverse while the embedding continues
to move in a similar direction. The shared finding is that
oscillation is visible in the learned function; its distribution
across depth depends on the architecture. An early observed
reversal identifies participation, not necessarily the layer that
caused it.

annotations.comment: Some notes I gathered discussing with the agent about the interpretation here: The word “mode” means a fixed pattern describing which representation coordinates change together, and in what proportions.For example, suppose a representation has three coordinates. One pattern could bev=(0.8, -0.6, 0).Moving along this pattern means the first coordinate increases while the second decreases, with the third unchanged. At a particular training step:- A coefficient of 2 produces the change (1.6,-1.2,0).- A coefficient of -1 produces the opposite change (-0.8,0.6,0).The pattern stays fixed; its strength and sign vary between steps. That fixed pattern is what we call a mode.The analysis finds these patterns by examining all changes in the selected window together. It chooses the first pattern to capture the greatest total squared movement. It then finds perpendicular patterns that capture the remaining movement.Thus, each actual representation change is reconstructed by adding several patterns, each with its own coefficient at that step.For our Transformer, the statement is:> Across the 49 updates, the representation changes can be closely reconstructed using 15 fixed patterns. Their changing coefficients describe how the network moves along those patterns over time.So “dominant patterns of representation change” is the clearer phrase. “Modes” is simply the mathematical shorthand for those patterns.  Worked for 24s • 09:23Ok, and this 15 fixed patterns of representation changes are evaluated accross thousands of samples, multiple steps, and multiple network dimensions. So, the functional change / oscilation is low-dimensional, right?Yes—the observed functional changes are approximately low-dimensional within the analyzed window. The same 15 patterns jointly describe movement across the reference inputs, output coordinates, and training steps.For the Transformer specifically, we analyze:- 64 reference sequences, containing 2,240 token positions;- the complete vocabulary-output vector at each position;- 49 consecutive representation changes.Across that entire collection, a 15-dimensional subspace captures 95% of the squared output movement. The signed coefficients then show repeated reversals along the dominant patterns. Together, these observations support low-dimensional, oscillatory movement of the measured function outputs, beyond an observation about gradients alone.Two qualifications make the statement precise:- The decomposition is computed separately for each measured stage. We have not established one shared 15-dimensional spatial subspace across all layers.- With 49 changes, the observed rank is already bounded by 49. The empirical concentration is 15 out of those 49 available directions, rather than simply “15 versus millions of coordinates.”A strong, accurate formulation is:> During the selected window, the Transformer’s output changes concentrate in a small set of representation-change patterns whose amplitudes repeatedly reverse, revealing structured oscillation in the learned function
